title: The pipe() Function and Pipeable Operators

options.text: A function that takes a source Observable and returns a new Observable
A method patched onto the Observable prototype
A plain value emitted by an Observable
A subscription callback

questions.explanation: A pipeable operator has the type OperatorFunction<T, R>: (source: Observable<T>) => Observable<R>. Calling a factory like map(fn) produces one.

questions.prompt: `source$.pipe(a, b, c)` is equivalent to which expression?

options.text: c(b(a(source$)))
a(b(c(source$)))
source$(a, b, c)
a(source$) + b(source$) + c(source$)

questions.explanation: pipe applies operators left to right: a first, then b on a's output, then c on b's output — i.e. c(b(a(source))).

questions.prompt: After `const doubled$ = nums$.pipe(map(n => n * 2))`, what is true of `nums$`?

options.text: nums$ is unchanged and still emits its original values
nums$ now emits doubled values too, because pipe mutates it
nums$ can no longer be subscribed to
nums$ is converted into a Promise

questions.explanation: Operators are pure: pipe returns a NEW Observable (doubled$) and never mutates the source. nums$ still emits its original values and can be reused.

questions.prompt: Which statements about operators and pipe are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nothing runs until you subscribe to the piped Observable
Operator order can change the result
The standalone pipe() composes operators into one reusable operator
You must import operators by patching the Observable prototype

questions.explanation: Pipes are lazy descriptions, order matters, and standalone pipe() builds reusable operators. Prototype patching is the old, removed style — modern operators are pipeable and imported by name.

questions.prompt: In RxJS 7.2+, complete the modern import: `import { map, filter } from '______'`
questions.explanation: Since 7.2, pipeable operators are exported from the main 'rxjs' entry point. The legacy path 'rxjs/operators' still works for older code.

questions.prompt: Why is it usually better to place `filter` before an expensive `map` in a pipe?

options.text: So the expensive transform runs only on values that pass the filter
Because map cannot appear after filter
Because filter mutates the source first
It has no effect; order never matters

questions.explanation: Filtering first discards values early, so the costly map only processes survivors — avoiding wasted work.
